clue.text: Conservatory orchestra's finale slowly absorbs

indicators.note: the musical tempo word takes in another letter, so one piece swallows the other

parts.note: lento is the musical direction meaning slowly

indicators.note: a finale is the end, so the last letter of the word orchestra is taken

explanation.surface: A music school's orchestra plays its closing movement at a leisurely pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conservatory' looks like a music school to match orchestra, but it is the glass garden room. 'absorbs' puts A (the end of orchestra) inside LENTO.
explanation.definitionFit: A lean-to is a simple glazed extension against a house wall, which is what a conservatory often is.

clue.text: Show disgust for Times report of peers getting reward for failure

parts.note: to boo is to show disgust at a performer
by is used for times in multiplication, as in three by four

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the next word is taken as spoken

parts.note: to peer is to pry, so peers means pries, a word spoken the same as the last piece

explanation.surface: Readers jeer at the Times for reporting that members of the Lords are being honoured despite failing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper but is the multiplication sign read as BY; 'report of' tells you that PRIES, from 'peers', is heard as PRIZE.
explanation.definitionFit: A booby prize is a joke award given to whoever comes last in a contest.

clue.text: Bill may be in couple with seamy side

parts.note: a couple in a relationship is an item

indicators.note: seamy suggests something disreputable or bent out of shape, so the letters of side are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone named Bill might be caught up with a couple and shown in a disreputable light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name but is an invoice; 'seamy', meaning sordid, is the signal that rearranges the four letters after the couple.
explanation.definitionFit: An invoice can be broken down into individual listed charges, which is what a detailed account shows.

clue.text: An article, or three in different languages

parts.note: le is the French word for the, a definite article
a is the English indefinite article
der is the German word for the, a definite article

explanation.surface: A grammar note offers one article, or else three drawn from various tongues.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay strings together three grammatical articles: French LE, English A and German DER. The definition plays on the other sense of article, a piece in a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's leading article, its editorial, is called by this name in Britain.

clue.text: Belts that are worn by Hell's Angels

definitions.meaning: to belt someone is to thrash them, as is to give them a good beating with a strap

definitions.text: that are worn by Hell's Angels
definitions.meaning: bikers' heavy hide jackets and trousers

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means thrashes with a strap, and as a noun it is motorcyclists' protective hide clothing.

clue.text: Toxic condition of armpit — so revolting!

indicators.note: revolting means rising up and overturning, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A smelly underarm is so disgusting it amounts to poisoning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolting' looks like a description of the smell, but it is the signal to rearrange ARMPIT and SO.
explanation.definitionFit: Atropism is poisoning by atropine, the alkaloid found in deadly nightshade.

clue.text: Event for blues band's beginning with a track about love

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first pieces wrap around the zero for love
the beginning of a word is its first letter, here of band's

parts.note: a trace is a track or trail left behind
love is zero in tennis, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A gig for a blues group, starting with one number about romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blues' suggests music, but Oxford and Cambridge rowers are awarded Blues. 'about' puts O inside B plus A TRACE.
explanation.definitionFit: The annual Thames rowing contest between Oxford and Cambridge universities is raced by crews who earn Blues.

clue.text: Space for worshippers heading away from moral failure

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter, which goes away

parts.note: a lapse is a moral slip or failing

explanation.surface: Churchgoers lose their place when their leader suffers an ethical fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading away' drops the first letter of LAPSE.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the semicircular recess at the east end of a church, part of where a congregation gathers.

clue.text: What's stopping them making a literary work?

indicators.note: the letters that plug the gap across the two words are taken, sitting inside them

explanation.surface: A writer asks what is preventing people from producing a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's stopping' asks for the letters lodged inside 'them making', across the join of the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's novel of 1815 about a meddling matchmaker bears this title.

clue.text: Notorious diatribe by agitator in extremis

indicators.note: in extremis is read as at the extremes, so only the outermost letters of agitator are used

parts.note: a diatribe is a rant, an angry tirade

explanation.surface: A notorious troublemaker delivers a tirade when pushed to the limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in extremis' usually means in dire straits; here it takes the extreme letters, A and R, of agitator.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrant means utter or out-and-out, as in an arrant knave, a notorious rogue.

clue.text: Obama wrestling with problem requiring bit of guts

indicators.note: wrestling suggests the letters grappling and twisting into a new order

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: The President grapples with a difficult issue that needs some courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guts' suggests courage, but it means innards. 'wrestling' rearranges OBAMA into ABOMA.
explanation.definitionFit: The abomasum is the fourth chamber of a ruminant's stomach, so part of its digestive tract.

clue.text: Where St Augustine was at university, being something of a brain?

parts.note: Augustine was bishop of Hippo in North Africa
on campus means at university

explanation.surface: A question about the saint's student days, hinting at a great mind.
explanation.walkthrough: St Augustine of Hippo was a bishop in what is now Algeria, so Hippo is where he was.
explanation.definitionFit: The hippocampus is a ridge in each temporal lobe of the brain involved in memory.

clue.text: Soldiers putting on act — that's rank and file

indicators.note: the soldiers are put in among the other letters, which wrap around them
rank means foul or gone bad, so the letters of act and that are spoilt into a new order

parts.note: men is a common term for soldiers

explanation.surface: Troops staging a performance, which says something about the ordinary ranks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rank and file' reads as one phrase about ordinary troops; 'rank' is in fact the anagram signal, and the 's of 'that's' gives no letter. 'putting on' puts the soldiers inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An email can carry a document added to it, a sent file of that kind.

clue.text: Gather round fighter from Biblical region

indicators.note: the gathering word goes round the boxer, enclosing him

parts.note: to glean is to gather, as leftover grain
Muhammad Ali, the boxer

explanation.surface: Collect a warrior from the Holy Land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' looks like a boxing round to go with fighter, but it is the container signal: the gathering word wraps the boxer Muhammad Ali.
explanation.definitionFit: Galilee is the northern region of ancient Palestine; Galilean describes someone or something coming from there.

clue.text: Wonderful people Spooner invites to parties where there's much chatter

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words

parts.note: fab is slang for fabulous, wonderful
the people a host invites are guests

explanation.surface: A clergyman asks splendid folk along to sociable gatherings full of gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of FAB GUESTS to get the spelt word.
explanation.definitionFit: A gabfest is an informal gathering given over to lengthy talk and gossip.

clue.text: Like some gems? Rue cost that's ruinous

indicators.note: ruinous suggests wrecking the letters of the two words into a new form

explanation.surface: A jeweller regrets the crippling price of stones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruinous' seems to describe the cost but signals that RUE COST is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes diamonds shaped with a flat base and a domed top of triangular facets, an old cut.

clue.text: Disregard story, knocking back afternoon tea loudly

parts.note: a conte is a short story, especially a French one

indicators.note: knocking back means turning around, so the letters for afternoon are read in reverse

parts.note: PM is post meridiem, afternoon

indicators.note: loudly means spoken out, so the drink is given by its letter that sounds the same

parts.note: the drink tea sounds like the letter T

explanation.surface: Ignore the tale about downing a cuppa noisily in the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking back' looks like drinking the tea, but it reverses the afternoon abbreviation; 'loudly' turns tea into the letter that sounds like it. A conte is a French-style short tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Contempt is scorn, a lack of regard for someone or something.

clue.text: State of the Nation lacking relevance

parts.note: India is a nation
N/A stands for not applicable

explanation.surface: A speech on the State of the Nation that has no bearing on anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State of the Nation' reads as one phrase about a political speech; 'State' alone is the definition, an American state.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana is one of the fifty United States, in the Midwest.

clue.text: Cowboy could wear one down with two 4 acrosses

parts.note: to neck a drink is to down it quickly
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is a leader, the Queen
a chief is a leader

explanation.surface: A cowboy might put one on after downing a drink with a couple of bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: 4 across is LEADER, so two leaders are needed: ER, the Queen's royal cipher, and CHIEF.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy ties a cloth around the neck against dust and sun.

clue.text: Tesco's bananas for baby

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the name of the supermarket chain, the apostrophe giving no letter

explanation.surface: A British supermarket sells bananas suitable for infants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like fruit on sale but means mad, the anagram signal. Tesco is a large British supermarket chain.
explanation.definitionFit: To baby someone is to pamper or coddle them, which is to cosset them.

clue.text: Something suggestive of the rise of corporations

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading upwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: corporation is jocular slang for a large belly, a tum

explanation.surface: A hint that big business is growing in power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corporations' looks like big firms, but in old slang a corporation is a pot belly, so TUMS.
explanation.definitionFit: Smut is indecent, suggestive talk or material.

clue.text: Back out of moving in Italian town

indicators.note: the back of the word, its final letter, is taken out

parts.note: astir means up and moving about

explanation.surface: Someone withdraws from a move into a town in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back out of' looks like retreating from a deal; it drops the last letter of ASTIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a town in Piedmont, famed for its sparkling wine.

clue.text: Uses wrong words for male and female titles

parts.note: mister is the title for a man
Ms is a title for a woman

explanation.surface: Someone gets forms of address for men and women muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a verb phrase: to misterm is to name something wrongly.
explanation.definitionFit: To misterm is to call by an incorrect name, misnaming things.

clue.text: Disreputable business in the East End has groups of schoolkids on drugs

indicators.note: Cockneys of London's East End drop their aitches, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: the word has, spoken without its first letter
pupils are taught in ability groups called sets
tripping means high on hallucinogens

explanation.surface: A shady firm in East London has bands of pupils off their heads.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech, from London's East End, drops the H, so 'has' becomes AS. British schools group pupils by ability into sets.
explanation.definitionFit: Asset-stripping is buying a company to sell off its assets for profit, a practice widely seen as disreputable.

clue.text: See 23
It's played with wrong score the wrong way!

parts.note: a score can be a mark of ten, a perfect result in many contests

indicators.note: going the wrong way means backwards, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: a sin is a wrong

explanation.surface: A game is spoilt by a bad result on the scoreboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the wrong way' reverses the sin that comes before it in the clue; ten is a score in the sense of a mark out of ten.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis is a racket sport played on a court, a game people play.
